# Chapter 8 - sketch answers {.unnumbered}

\(1\) The criteria are the measuring instruments: Fixed in advance, they make
every rating comparable and honest. Set afterwards, they invite bias - the
scale gets bent so the results look the way someone wants ("let's call that
medium"). (2) The customer database and the order process are primary -
information and a business process. The cloud hosting and the developer are
supporting - infrastructure and a person the primary assets depend on; if
either fails, the primary assets fail with them. (3) Spoofing: A fake checkout
page harvesting logins. Tampering: Altering prices or order totals in transit.
Repudiation: A customer denies an order and no audit log exists. Information
disclosure: Payment details exposed in transit. Denial of service: The checkout
flooded offline (R2). Elevation of privilege: A customer session reaching
administrative functions. (4) "No backups" names a missing control - a
vulnerability - but no source, event, asset or harm, so it cannot be rated.
Rewritten: A ransomware operator encrypts the order and customer data,
exploiting the absence of tested backups, so that FastGoods cannot restore and
loses both sales and data - prolonged outage and permanent data loss as the
consequence. (5) From the process, step *pay*: An attacker floods the checkout,
exploiting the absence of dedicated DDoS protection, so the shop cannot sell -
lost revenue; source: The order process, walked step by step. From a control,
cloud backups read backwards: They exist against data loss; tested, they have
never been restored, so the control is operating ineffectively and the risk
stands - a ransomware incident encrypts the order data, exploiting the
untested restore, and FastGoods cannot recover: Prolonged outage; source: An
existing control, read backwards and tested. (6) Recon: The attacker scans
FastGoods' public systems and finds an exposed administrative interface
(weakness: Unnecessary exposure). Delivery/exploit: A phishing mail to staff
yields admin credentials (weaknesses: Phishable staff, no MFA on admin logins).
Move: The attacker reaches the database with those rights (weakness: Excessive
access rights, no segmentation). Act: The customer table is exported (weakness:
No exfiltration monitoring, data unencrypted). (7) Why active? Nobody disabled
it. Why? IT was not told of the departure. Why? No leaver process connects HR
and IT. Root cause: A missing joiner/leaver process - fixing it prevents the
whole class of orphaned-access risks, not just this account. (8) Threat:
Credential stuffing is constant, automated and profitable - highly active.
Exposure: The login is internet-facing. Controls: Password-only authentication
- weak barrier. Conclusion: "Likely." Internal evidence: Failed-login spikes
in the authentication logs; external: Breach statistics and CTI reporting on
credential-stuffing campaigns against retail. (9) New external entity "analytics
provider" outside the circle; one arrow from FastGoods.com to it, labelled "page
views, session and device data" - and, if the widget sets identifiers,
personal data, so the arrow is purple. The flow admits tampering, disclosure and
denial; the survivor is disclosure: The analytics provider, or anyone reading
its script, receives customer behaviour and identifiers FastGoods never
assessed, exploiting an unreviewed third-party script on the shop page, exposing
personal data - a GDPR breach and, given the Magecart pattern of Chapter 7, a
route to card data. Work follows in Chapter 9 (a new recipient in the Article 30
record; a DPIA screening question) and Chapter 19 (a new supplier to tier and
contract). (10) Asset register: Order database - owner Ops, I high, A high.
DFD: D2 Order DB, data tier behind TB2, written by the checkout, read and
written by the back office. Risk register: R2's consequence flows through it (no
orders written while the checkout is down); a tampering candidate from the
per-element pass. Article 30 record: Order history - names, addresses,
purchases - purpose contract performance, basis Art. 6(1)(b), retention per
the bookkeeping rules. SoA: 8.13 backups, 8.15 logging, 8.3 access restriction,
justified by R2 and the tampering candidate. EA repository: Data object "order"
realised by an artifact on the same node as D1. Lost with two names: The chain
- the auditor cannot show that the backup evidenced in the SoA is the store
the register rates, so the control cannot be tied to the risk.
